scenes.title: King Edward and Harold
scenes.latinInscription: EDVVARD REX :
scenes.englishTranslation: King Edward.
scenes.summary: King Edward sits enthroned and speaks with two men; the standing noble nearest him is conventionally identified as Harold Godwinson. The embroidery does not record the substance of their exchange.

annotations.title: The enthroned king
annotations.preview: Edward’s gesture begins the narrative, but not its explanation.
annotations.commentary: Edward is framed by palace architecture and gestures toward the standing noble usually identified as Harold. Because no caption states what Edward commands, any precise diplomatic mission belongs to later interpretation, not direct observation.

annotations.title: A restored opening name
annotations.preview: The name EDVVARD is probably not eleventh-century stitching.
annotations.commentary: The word EDVVARD is visible today but is absent from early eighteenth-century copies. Musset and later commentators therefore treat the name as a restoration; REX anchors the royal identification independently.

scenes.title: Harold Rides to Bosham
scenes.latinInscription: VBI : hAROLD DVX : ANGLORVM : ET SVI MILITES : EQVITANT : AD BOShAM :
scenes.englishTranslation: Where Harold, leader of the English, and his soldiers ride to Bosham.
scenes.summary: Harold travels toward Bosham with mounted companions, hunting birds and running hounds. The procession establishes his elite status before the Channel crossing.

annotations.title: Hawk and hounds
annotations.preview: Elite travel is signalled by aristocratic hunting animals.
annotations.commentary: Harold carries a hawk while hounds run among the horses. These animals mark the company as aristocratic, but they do not by themselves prove that the journey’s purpose was hunting.

annotations.title: Dux Anglorum
annotations.preview: The caption calls Harold dux of the English.
annotations.commentary: Dux is literally a leader and can carry the sense of earl or military commander here. Translating it mechanically as a continental-style ‘duke’ can imply a title that Harold did not formally hold.

scenes.title: Bosham Church and Feast
scenes.latinInscription: ECCLESIA :
scenes.englishTranslation: The church.
scenes.summary: Harold’s party approaches a church at Bosham and then eats in an upper hall before embarking. The scene compresses devotional, domestic and logistical moments into one continuous passage.

annotations.title: The church at Bosham
annotations.preview: The single word ECCLESIA labels the compact church image.
annotations.commentary: The preceding caption supplies Bosham, while ECCLESIA simply identifies the building as a church. Its form should be read as medieval pictorial architecture, not as a measured portrait of a surviving structure.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 03.

annotations.title: Fables beneath the departure
annotations.preview: Animal fables begin to accompany Harold’s outward journey.
annotations.commentary: The lower border around the Bosham meal and embarkation begins a sustained run of Aesopic material. Scholars disagree over whether these fables comment directly on Harold’s conduct or operate more loosely as thematic counterpoint.

scenes.title: Harold Sets Sail
scenes.latinInscription: HIC hAROLD : MARE NAVIGAVIT :
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Harold sailed the sea.
scenes.summary: Men leave the hall, carry equipment to the shore and board a vessel for the Channel crossing. Harold’s reason for sailing is left unstated by both image and caption.

annotations.title: Wading to the ship
annotations.preview: Bare-legged travellers carry gear through shallow water.
annotations.commentary: Several men hitch up their garments and wade out to the vessel, conveying the practical work of embarkation. The ship’s overlapping oars, steering gear and curved hull are valuable visual evidence, though not a technical plan.

annotations.title: An unstated mission
annotations.preview: The embroidery never says why Harold crosses the Channel.
annotations.commentary: Later Norman accounts frame the voyage as a mission connected with William’s succession claim, while English traditions permit other readings. The scene introduces these competing narratives, but the caption does not choose between them.

scenes.title: With Full Sails to Ponthieu
scenes.latinInscription: ET VELIS : VENTO : PLENIS VENIT : IN TERRA : VVIDONIS COMITIS
scenes.englishTranslation: And with sails full of wind he came into the land of Count Wido.
scenes.summary: Harold’s vessels cross the Channel under full sail and reach the territory of Count Wido, Guy of Ponthieu. The embroidery names the destination but does not show or mention a storm.

annotations.title: Sails full of wind
annotations.preview: The caption and bulging sails agree on a wind-driven crossing.
annotations.commentary: The phrase velis vento plenis is unusually specific: the sails are ‘full of wind.’ It supports a vigorous passage but does not by itself tell us whether Harold intended to land in Ponthieu.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 05.

annotations.title: The land of Count Wido
annotations.preview: Wido is the Latin form used for Guy of Ponthieu.
annotations.commentary: The caption identifies the coast politically rather than geographically: this is ‘the land of Count Wido.’ Guy’s authority over the landing place prepares the capture that follows.

scenes.title: Harold Comes Ashore
scenes.latinInscription: HAROLD :
scenes.englishTranslation: Harold.
scenes.summary: Harold stands in the beached vessel holding a hawk as members of his party step into shallow water. Armed men wait on shore, linking the landing directly to the seizure in the next scene.

annotations.title: Harold identified
annotations.preview: A single stitched name fixes Harold’s position in the crowded landing.
annotations.commentary: The name HAROLD sits above the leading figure in the vessel, who still carries his hawk. This explicit label is especially useful because dress and hairstyle alone are not always reliable identifiers across the work.

annotations.title: Arrival meets arrest
annotations.preview: The landing and apprehension are visually continuous.
annotations.commentary: The hull runs almost into the waiting armed figures, leaving little neutral space between travel and detention. The painted scene numbers are later aids and do not necessarily match the original designer’s visual units.

scenes.title: Guy Seizes Harold
scenes.latinInscription: hIC : APREhENDIT : VVIDO : HAROLDṼ :
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Wido seized Harold.
scenes.summary: Guy of Ponthieu’s men take hold of Harold while Guy directs the action from horseback. The scene depicts detention through gesture and escort rather than a pitched struggle.

annotations.title: The act of seizure
annotations.preview: Hands on Harold’s upper body make the caption visible as action.
annotations.commentary: Two figures restrain Harold as an armed rider points toward him. The embroidery’s APREhENDIT has one P, an orthographic detail that normalized Latin often silently changes.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 07.

annotations.title: A high-status captive
annotations.preview: Harold is guarded and escorted, not shown bound in chains.
annotations.commentary: The controlled encounter suits the capture of an aristocratic traveller whose person had political and material value. The image alone cannot establish the precise legal terms of his detention or ransom.

scenes.title: Harold Is Taken to Beaurain
scenes.latinInscription: ET DVXIT : EVM AD BELREM : ET IBI EVM : TENVIT :
scenes.englishTranslation: And he led him to Beaurain and held him there.
scenes.summary: An armed mounted escort conducts Harold inland to Beaurain, named BELREM in the caption. The long procession turns captivity into movement rather than showing a prison interior.

annotations.title: The mounted escort
annotations.preview: Closely packed riders carry the narrative inland.
annotations.commentary: Spears, shields and overlapping horses identify an organised armed escort. The caption supplies the destination and detention; the figures themselves show transit rather than confinement.

annotations.title: Belrem is Beaurain
annotations.preview: The embroidered place-name uses a medieval form of Beaurain.
annotations.commentary: BELREM is conventionally identified with Beaurain in Ponthieu. The spelling is evidence for the caption’s linguistic world, not an error that should be replaced in the diplomatic text.

scenes.title: Harold and Guy Confer
scenes.latinInscription: VBI : hAROLD : ⁊ VVIDO : PARABOLANT :
scenes.englishTranslation: Where Harold and Wido converse.
scenes.summary: Harold stands before the seated Guy of Ponthieu while attendants cluster around them. Pointing hands and Guy’s upright sword make the exchange visibly formal and unequal.

annotations.title: A conversation in gestures
annotations.preview: Pointing hands animate a dialogue whose words are lost.
annotations.commentary: Guy sits with a sword upright while Harold and attendants gesture toward him. The posture establishes Guy’s local authority, but the subject and outcome of the conversation are not supplied.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 09.

annotations.title: The word PARABOLANT
annotations.preview: A characteristically medieval verb means ‘they converse.’
annotations.commentary: PARABOLANT is not classical idiom; it belongs to the developing medieval Latin vocabulary related to speech. The stitched ⁊ is the Tironian sign for et, ‘and.’

scenes.title: William’s Messengers Reach Guy
scenes.latinInscription:
VBI : NVNTII : VVILLELMI : DVCIS : VENERVNT : AD VVIDONE
TVROLD
scenes.englishTranslation: Where the messengers of Duke William came to Wido. Turold.
scenes.summary: Two envoys sent by Duke William confront Guy’s party over Harold’s detention. The separate name TVROLD appears beside a small horse-handler, but exactly whom it labels remains contested.

annotations.title: William’s envoys
annotations.preview: Pointing figures turn Harold’s capture into a negotiation.
annotations.commentary: The two standing envoys face Guy’s representative with assertive gestures and visible weapons. The caption confirms their sender but gives neither their spoken demand nor Guy’s response.

annotations.title: Who is Turold?
annotations.preview: The name may label the small figure or a nearby envoy.
annotations.commentary: TVROLD is positioned over a diminutive person holding the horses, encouraging the traditional identification. Other scholars attach it to the neighbouring messenger; proposed biographies and roles remain hypotheses.

scenes.title: William’s Messengers Ride
scenes.latinInscription: NVNTII : VVILLELMI
scenes.englishTranslation: The messengers of William.
scenes.summary: Two mounted envoys gallop at speed, their hair and cloaks reinforcing the urgency of the mission. The episode appears after their arrival at Guy’s court, creating a celebrated problem of narrative order.

annotations.title: A galloping embassy
annotations.preview: Extended horses and streaming hair convey speed.
annotations.commentary: The paired riders are compressed into a fast-moving group between architectural markers. Their shields and weapons indicate that diplomatic travel could also be armed travel.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 11.

annotations.title: A reverse-order episode
annotations.preview: The ride is shown after the envoys have already arrived.
annotations.commentary: Scenes 10–12 have prompted competing explanations: flashback, simultaneous action, or a reading that follows different figures across the cloth. Wissolik’s proposed solution is influential but has not eliminated the ambiguity.

scenes.title: News Reaches Duke William
scenes.latinInscription: † hIC VENIT : NVNTIVS : AD WILGELMVM DVCEM
scenes.englishTranslation: Here a messenger came to Duke William.
scenes.summary: A messenger reports to William, who is seated beneath an architectural canopy. A stitched cross immediately before the caption is visually conspicuous but not securely explained.

annotations.title: William’s first appearance
annotations.preview: The duke receives news from an approaching messenger.
annotations.commentary: William sits elevated while the messenger reaches toward him, visually establishing command before Harold is brought into his presence. The caption names William but not the reporter or the message.

annotations.title: The cross before HIC
annotations.preview: A cross-like sign may mark a production or textual boundary.
annotations.commentary: The sign is stitched into the caption zone rather than painted on the backing. Scholars have connected it with sectioning, correction or a change in working practice, but no single explanation is secure.

scenes.title: Guy Brings Harold to William
scenes.latinInscription: HIC : WIDO : AD DVXIT hAROLDVM AD VVILGELMVM : NORMANNORVM : DVCEM
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Wido brought Harold to William, duke of the Normans.
scenes.summary: Guy escorts Harold to Duke William in an extended mounted procession. The caption’s unusual separation AD DVXIT is retained in the diplomatic transcription and normalized as ADDUXIT for reading.

annotations.title: A transfer of custody
annotations.preview: The mounted procession delivers Harold from Guy to William.
annotations.commentary: The caption makes Guy the active subject who brings Harold to William. It does not state whether William paid ransom, threatened Guy or relied on customary obligation, so those mechanisms should remain outside the core text.

annotations.preview: William receives an expansive territorial title.
annotations.commentary: NORMANNORVM DVCEM calls William ‘duke of the Normans.’ Across the first half of the embroidery he remains DUX, while royal language is reserved for Edward and later Harold.

scenes.title: William and Harold at the Palace
scenes.latinInscription: HIC : DVX : VVILGELM : CVM hAROLDO : VENIT : AD PALATIṼ SVṼ
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William came with Harold to his palace.
scenes.summary: William and Harold enter an elaborate hall where the seated duke receives a gesturing Harold. Rouen is often proposed as the setting, but the stitched caption says only ‘his palace.’

annotations.title: An unnamed palace
annotations.preview: The caption identifies function, not location.
annotations.commentary: Arcades, towers and a roof frame the ducal audience as a palace interior and exterior at once. Rouen is a plausible historical identification, but the embroidery itself does not name the city.

annotations.title: Harold before the seated duke
annotations.preview: Contrasting poses establish the courtly hierarchy.
annotations.commentary: William sits while Harold stands and gestures broadly, with armed attendants behind him. The scene conveys audience and negotiation but records no spoken terms.

scenes.title: The Cleric and Ælfgyva
scenes.latinInscription: VBI : VNVS : CLERICVS : ET : ÆLFGYVA
scenes.englishTranslation: Where a certain cleric and Ælfgyva.
scenes.summary: A cleric reaches toward the face of a woman named Ælfgyva beneath an incomplete, verbless caption. The episode’s people, action and relevance to the surrounding narrative remain unresolved.

annotations.title: A caption without a verb
annotations.preview: The inscription names two people but does not say what happens.
annotations.commentary: The cleric touches or gestures at Ælfgyva’s face, but the grammar stops after their names. Proposed identifications with several historical women and proposed readings as betrothal, rebuke or scandal remain speculative.

annotations.title: The mimicking nude figure
annotations.preview: A naked man below echoes the cleric’s raised arm.
annotations.commentary: The lower-border figure is frontal, naked and placed near the main-register encounter. Its visual echo has encouraged sexual or scandalous interpretations, but proximity and resemblance do not identify a specific lost story.

scenes.title: Toward Mont-Saint-Michel
scenes.latinInscription: hIC VVILLEM : DVX : ET EXERCITVS : EIVS : VENERVNT : AD MONTĒ MICHAELIS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William and his army came to the Mount of Michael.
scenes.summary: William’s mounted force, with Harold among it, reaches Mont-Saint-Michel on the way into Brittany. The abbey-crowned mount acts as both a place label and a major visual landmark.

annotations.title: The Mount of Michael
annotations.preview: A church crowns the embroidered tidal mount.
annotations.commentary: The distinctive mound and sanctuary make Mont-Saint-Michel legible even before the caption is translated. The image is symbolic and compressed rather than a reliable reconstruction of the eleventh-century abbey.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 16.

annotations.title: Harold joins William’s campaign
annotations.preview: The former captive now rides with the ducal army.
annotations.commentary: The caption calls the company William’s exercitus, his army, and the narrative places Harold within it. Whether this reflects willing alliance, honourable hospitality or constrained participation is not stated.

scenes.title: Crossing the Couesnon
scenes.latinInscription:
ET hIC : TRANSIERVNT : FLVMEN : COSNONIS :
hIC : hAROLD : DVX : TRAhEBAT : EOS : DE ARENA
scenes.englishTranslation: And here they crossed the River Couesnon. Here Harold the earl was pulling them from the sand.
scenes.summary: The army crosses the Couesnon estuary, where men struggle in soft sand and water. Harold carries one man and pulls another free, receiving an emphatically heroic role.

annotations.title: The dangerous river crossing
annotations.preview: Raised clothing and lifted shields show men negotiating water and sand.
annotations.commentary: The wavy ground line and awkward postures distinguish the Couesnon crossing from ordinary mounted travel. The caption explicitly names both the river and the sand.

annotations.title: Harold the rescuer
annotations.preview: Harold saves two men at once and dominates the centre.
annotations.commentary: The embroidery enlarges Harold and gives him extraordinary physical agency, carrying one man while hauling another from the sand. Scholars differ on whether this admiration builds a tragic hero or simply records exemplary service to William.

scenes.title: Conan Flees Dol
scenes.latinInscription:
ET VENERVNT AD DOL : ET : CONAN : FVGA VERTIT :
REDNES
scenes.englishTranslation: And they came to Dol, and Conan turned in flight. Rennes.
scenes.summary: At Dol, Conan escapes down a rope from a timber-topped stronghold as William’s force advances. The small label REDNES marks Rennes and carries the itinerary onward.

annotations.title: Conan’s rope descent
annotations.preview: The Breton duke leaves Dol by a rope from the fortification.
annotations.commentary: Conan’s body hangs outside the tower while mounted troops approach, turning the caption’s ‘flight’ into a vivid humiliation. Whether the rope escape records an event or sharpens partisan storytelling cannot be established.

annotations.title: Dol and Rennes as landmarks
annotations.preview: Compact strongholds punctuate the march through Brittany.
annotations.commentary: The buildings organise space and identify stops rather than supplying literal town portraits. Pastan cautions that medieval architectural images combine convention, narrative function and selective local memory.

scenes.title: The Attack on Dinan
scenes.latinInscription: hIC MILITES VVILLELMI : DVCIS : PVGNANT : CONTRA DINANTES :
scenes.englishTranslation: Here the soldiers of Duke William fight against the people of Dinan.
scenes.summary: William’s mounted soldiers attack Dinan while defenders crowd a raised timber enclosure. Men beneath the fortification apply fire to its wooden elements.

annotations.title: Cavalry at the walls
annotations.preview: Mounted attackers close on Dinan’s elevated defences.
annotations.commentary: The riders carry spears and shields into a tightly compressed assault. The image shows the attackers’ momentum, but it should not be treated as a complete tactical record of a siege.

annotations.title: Fire against timber
annotations.preview: Two armoured men threaten the wooden enclosure with flames.
annotations.commentary: The attackers beneath the structure hold firebrands toward its timbers, making combustibility central to the scene. The architecture is narratively legible but not a construction drawing of Dinan’s actual defences.

scenes.title: Conan Surrenders Dinan
scenes.latinInscription: ET : CVNAN : CLAVES : PORREXIT :
scenes.englishTranslation: And Conan held out the keys.
scenes.summary: Conan extends the keys of Dinan from the fortification toward the mounted victors. The keys are transferred across the gap on the ends of long weapons or staffs.

annotations.title: The keys of Dinan
annotations.preview: A compact bunch of keys makes surrender visible.
annotations.commentary: The keys hang between the opposing parties, exactly matching the caption’s CLAVES. Their conspicuous isolation turns an abstract transfer of control into a readable object-centred action.

annotations.preview: The exchange is mediated by long shafts rather than hand-to-hand contact.
annotations.commentary: Conan and the mounted recipient remain physically separated while the keys bridge the space. This may dramatise caution or ceremonial transfer, but the image does not establish a standard legal ritual.

scenes.title: William Gives Harold Arms
scenes.latinInscription: hIC : WILLELM : DEDIT : hAROLDO : ARMA
scenes.englishTranslation: Here William gave arms to Harold.
scenes.summary: William formally presents military equipment to Harold after the Breton campaign. The gesture has often been read as honour, investiture or a sign of a new lord–man relationship, but the caption says only that arms were given.

annotations.title: The gift of arms
annotations.preview: Two mailed figures enact a formal transfer of military status.
annotations.commentary: William and Harold stand face to face in mail while weapons frame the exchange. Their isolation from the mounted column gives the action ceremonial emphasis.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 21.

annotations.title: Honour or vassalage?
annotations.preview: The social meaning of the gift is debated.
annotations.commentary: Some readings treat the arms as William’s reward for Harold’s service; others see investiture that places Harold under William. Legal-symbolic gestures were context-dependent, and the embroidery provides no accompanying formula.

scenes.title: William Comes to Bayeux
scenes.latinInscription: hIE VVILLELM VENIT : BAGIAS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here William came to Bayeux.
scenes.summary: William rides through an architectural gateway labelled by the caption as Bayeux. The embroidered HIE is normally understood as a slip for HIC, ‘here.’

annotations.title: HIE, not HIC
annotations.preview: The embroidery preserves a small but famous spelling anomaly.
annotations.commentary: The first word is visibly hIE. Editors generally understand it as HIC, but the diplomatic text should retain the stitched form rather than silently repairing it.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 22.

annotations.title: Why Bayeux?
annotations.preview: The embroidery’s location differs from William of Poitiers’s account.
annotations.commentary: The tapestry places the coming oath at Bayeux, whereas William of Poitiers locates Harold’s oath at Bonneville. Scholars have linked the choice of Bayeux to local relics and to theories about Bishop Odo’s role, but the motive remains debated.

scenes.title: Harold Swears the Oath
scenes.latinInscription: VBI hAROLD : SACRAMENTVM : FECIT : VVILLELMO DVCI :
scenes.englishTranslation: Where Harold made an oath to Duke William.
scenes.summary: Harold stands between two reliquary supports and extends a hand to each while William watches enthroned. The image stresses the oath’s sacred setting but does not state the promise’s exact terms.

annotations.title: Hands on two reliquaries
annotations.preview: Harold’s outstretched hands make the oath physically explicit.
annotations.commentary: The containers are presented as sacred supports or reliquaries, one on each side of Harold. Their crosses and elevated placement make violation of the oath a religious as well as political matter within the Norman story.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 23.

annotations.title: An oath without stated terms
annotations.preview: SACRAMENTVM names the act, not the promise.
annotations.commentary: Norman narratives say Harold supported William’s succession claim; other traditions dispute the circumstances and binding force. The embroidery neither quotes an oath formula nor acknowledges coercion, so both content and consent require sourced explanation.

scenes.title: Harold Returns to England
scenes.latinInscription: hIC hAROLD : DVX : REVERSVS : EST AD ANGLICAM : TERRAM :
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Harold the earl returned to England.
scenes.summary: Harold sails back across the Channel and is sighted from an English shore building. The movement reverses the outward voyage while the caption restores Harold’s title DUX.

annotations.title: The homeward ship
annotations.preview: A crowded vessel carries Harold back toward England.
annotations.commentary: The sail, steering oar and tightly seated crew repeat visual language from the outward crossing. The caption, not the ship type, establishes that the destination is English land.

annotations.preview: A lookout peers from a raised building toward the arriving ship.
annotations.commentary: The figure shades or raises a hand while looking seaward, bridging voyage and homecoming. The compact architecture functions as a narrative marker rather than a securely identifiable port portrait.

scenes.title: Harold Returns to King Edward
scenes.latinInscription: ET VENIT : AD : EDVVARDVM REGEM :
scenes.englishTranslation: And he came to King Edward.
scenes.summary: Harold stands before Edward after returning from Normandy, while the seated king raises a hand in response. Neither caption nor image records what Harold reports or how Edward judges it.

annotations.title: Harold before Edward
annotations.preview: The returning earl gestures toward the enthroned king.
annotations.commentary: Edward’s raised hand and Harold’s extended arms communicate an intense audience, but gestures in the embroidery do not translate into exact dialogue. Descriptions such as confession or rebuke should therefore be framed as readings.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 25.

annotations.title: What did Harold report?
annotations.preview: The tapestry leaves the meeting’s content blank.
annotations.commentary: A Norman reading can make Harold’s oath the subject of the audience, but that conclusion depends on reconstructing a chain of events from later texts. White cautions against treating such reconstructions as the embroidery’s unambiguous record.

scenes.title: Edward’s Funeral Procession
scenes.latinInscription: hIC PORTATVR : CORPVS : EADVVARDI : REGIS : AD : ECCLESIAM : S̅C̅I PETRI APL̅I
scenes.englishTranslation: Here the body of King Edward is carried to the church of Saint Peter the Apostle.
scenes.summary: Edward’s body is carried toward his newly built Westminster Abbey as clergy and mourners follow. The procession is shown before the deathbed scene, a deliberate or meaningful disruption of chronological order.

annotations.title: The royal funeral
annotations.preview: Eight bearers carry Edward’s richly covered bier toward the abbey.
annotations.commentary: The procession moves leftward, briefly reversing the tapestry’s usual visual flow, and clergy ring handbells behind the bier. This placement brings Edward’s burial into direct contact with the deathbed and succession scenes.

annotations.title: A newly consecrated Westminster Abbey
annotations.preview: God’s hand blesses the church while a workman tends its roof.
annotations.commentary: Edward’s church was consecrated on 28 December 1065, when the king was already too ill to attend; he died on 5 January 1066. The descending hand and roof-top worker visually stress a sacred building only just completed.

scenes.title: Edward on His Deathbed
scenes.latinInscription: hIC EADVVARDVS : REX IN LECTO : ALLOQVIT : FIDELES :
scenes.englishTranslation: Here King Edward, in bed, addresses his faithful followers.
scenes.summary: The dying Edward reaches toward a kneeling figure conventionally identified as Harold while Queen Edith mourns at the foot of the bed. The gesture became central to competing claims about whom Edward intended to succeed him.

annotations.title: The deathbed group
annotations.preview: Edward, Edith, Harold and attendants occupy a compressed upper room.
annotations.commentary: Edward lies crowned and half-upright; Edith is placed at his feet and a kneeling man receives his extended hand. The identities of Harold and Edith are supported by narrative context and related texts rather than separate stitched labels.

citationDetails.locator: Official numbered panorama, scene 27; same embroidered compartment as scene 28.

annotations.title: A gesture of designation?
annotations.preview: Edward’s touch has been read as entrusting the kingdom to Harold.
annotations.commentary: The near-contemporary Vita Ædwardi reports Edward commending Edith and the kingdom to Harold’s protection. The embroidery records the hand-to-hand gesture but no words, so its legal force and its relationship to earlier promises remain disputed.

scenes.title: Edward’s Body Is Prepared
scenes.latinInscription: ET hIC : DEFVNCTVS EST
scenes.englishTranslation: And here he died.
scenes.summary: Below the deathbed, attendants prepare Edward’s body in a shroud while a cleric stands nearby. Living and dead king occupy the same architectural compartment, compressing time into a single image.

annotations.title: The shrouded king
annotations.preview: Attendants wrap or sew Edward’s body for burial.
annotations.commentary: The dead king lies horizontal beneath the still-living Edward above, with workers attending to the patterned covering. The physical preparation of the corpse links the private death chamber to the public funeral already shown.

annotations.title: Living and dead at once
annotations.preview: Two temporal states share one architectural frame.
annotations.commentary: The stacked registers make Edward simultaneously the speaking king and the prepared corpse. Thompson reads this dense temporal construction as an invitation to reflect on kingship in death, not as a simple chronological mistake.

scenes.title: The Crown Is Given to Harold
scenes.latinInscription: hIC DEDERVNT : hAROLDO : CORONÃ : REGIS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here they gave Harold the king’s crown.
scenes.summary: Two men present Harold with a crown and a long-handled axe, the regalia of the kingship he is about to assume. The composition places this transfer immediately beside Edward’s death chamber.

annotations.title: Crown and ceremonial axe
annotations.preview: The regalia identify the transfer of royal office.
annotations.commentary: A crowned object is held toward Harold while another figure carries the long-handled axe associated with late Anglo-Saxon royal power. The caption’s plural verb, DEDERVNT, corresponds to the group action.

annotations.title: Who gives the crown?
annotations.preview: The presenters are usually read as leading English nobles or the witan.
annotations.commentary: The embroidery does not name the two presenters or depict a complete assembly. Identifying them with representatives of the witan is historically plausible, but the image should not be made to prove a modern constitutional model of election.

scenes.title: Harold Enthroned
scenes.latinInscription: hIC RЄSIDET hAROLD RЄX ANGLORVM
scenes.englishTranslation: Here sits Harold, king of the English.
scenes.summary: Harold sits crowned on an elevated throne, holding the emblems of rule while courtiers acclaim him. The composition presents royal authority while the surrounding sequence keeps his succession politically charged.

annotations.title: The signs of kingship
annotations.preview: Crown, throne and hand-held regalia make Harold unmistakably royal.
annotations.commentary: The scene does not show a tentative claimant: Harold is fully enthroned and equipped with royal insignia. That clarity matters because the tapestry can acknowledge his effective kingship while still framing the route by which he obtained it as contested.

annotations.title: “Here sits Harold”
annotations.preview: The caption describes enthronement, not the act of crowning.
annotations.commentary: RESIDET is a present-tense statement that Harold 'sits' as king. The actual transfer of the crown belongs to the preceding scene, so image and caption emphasize the achieved condition of rule.

scenes.title: Archbishop Stigand
scenes.latinInscription: STIGANT ARChIEPISCOPVS
scenes.englishTranslation: Stigand, archbishop.
scenes.summary: Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, stands beside the enthroned Harold and is identified by name and office. His presence has long shaped debate about the legitimacy and officiant of Harold's coronation.

annotations.title: A named archbishop
annotations.preview: The titulus fixes the adjacent churchman as Stigand.
annotations.commentary: Names are used sparingly in the embroidery, so identifying STIGANT and his rank gives the figure unusual interpretive weight. He stands next to Harold but is not shown placing the crown on his head.

annotations.title: Who crowned Harold?
annotations.preview: Stigand's proximity is suggestive, but the image never shows him crowning Harold.
annotations.commentary: Norman and later English traditions disagree over whether Stigand or Ealdred of York officiated. The embroidery's juxtaposition can cast suspicion on Harold's legitimacy without resolving the historical question, so the inference must remain explicitly contested.

scenes.title: The Comet
scenes.latinInscription: ISTI MIRANT STELLA
scenes.englishTranslation: These men marvel at a star.
scenes.summary: A group points upward at a blazing, tailed object now identified as Halley's Comet. Placed directly after Harold's accession, the apparition functions visually as a portent even though the caption calls it only a 'star.'

annotations.title: Halley's Comet in 1066
annotations.preview: The 'star' has the bright head and streaming tail of a comet.
annotations.commentary: Modern astronomy identifies the object as 1P/Halley, whose 1066 appearance became one of the embroidery's best-known details. The caption itself remains observational—people marvel at a stella—and does not name Halley or explicitly call the object a comet.

annotations.title: Wonder becomes warning
annotations.preview: Repeated pointing hands pull the viewer's eye from the crowd to the sky.
annotations.commentary: The placement after Harold's enthronement makes the comet easy to read as an ominous response to his kingship. That political or providential meaning is an interpretation created by sequence and gesture, not a meaning stated in the Latin.

scenes.title: Harold Receives Tidings
scenes.latinInscription: hAROLD
scenes.englishTranslation: Harold.
scenes.summary: Harold is named as he receives alarming news in the wake of the comet's appearance. Empty ships in the lower border echo the sea-borne threat that will soon move into the main narrative.

annotations.title: A king under pressure
annotations.preview: Harold's compact label leaves the gestures to carry the story.
annotations.commentary: Unlike the full verbal captions around it, this titulus supplies only Harold's name. The messenger's approach and Harold's response therefore link this moment back to the comet and forward to the invasion through visual narration.

annotations.title: Ships below the throne
annotations.preview: The lower border can be read as anticipating invasion by sea.
annotations.commentary: The border is not merely a frame: elsewhere it echoes, inverts and intensifies the central story. Reading these ships as a forecast of William's fleet is plausible, but the embroidery gives no caption that confirms this specific symbolism.

scenes.title: An English Ship Reaches Normandy
scenes.latinInscription: hIC NAVIS ANGLICA VЄNIT. IN TЄRRAM VWILLELMI  DVCIS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here an English ship came into the land of Duke William.
scenes.summary: An English ship reaches William’s territory. Its position before the shipbuilding scene invites a connection with the English succession, but the caption does not state its message.

annotations.title: The 'English ship'
annotations.preview: ANGLICA marks the vessel's origin directly in the caption.
annotations.commentary: The adjective is unusually specific and makes the ship itself the agent connecting Harold's England to William's Normandy. The caption says nothing about the messenger's identity or exact message.

annotations.title: A voyage as an ellipsis
annotations.preview: One ship compresses the transmission of news into a single crossing.
annotations.commentary: The embroidery repeatedly uses travel to create cause and effect. Here it omits deliberation in England and lets the ship carry the viewer directly into William's response.

scenes.title: William Orders Ships Built
scenes.latinInscription: HIC VVILLЄLM DVX IVSSIT NAVЄS EDIFICARE
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William ordered ships to be built.
scenes.summary: William issues the command for an invasion fleet, and the image flows directly into timber-felling and shipbuilding. Council, command and labour are joined in one rapidly advancing sequence.

annotations.title: Command in gesture
annotations.preview: Pointing hands connect William's council to the work outside.
annotations.commentary: The caption attributes the order to William, while the seated figures' gestures direct attention forward toward the woodcutters. Some readings give Odo an especially forceful advisory role, but the image does not record the council's words.

annotations.title: From trees to fleet
annotations.preview: Axes, adzes, ribs and overlapping planks condense shipbuilding into view.
annotations.commentary: The workers fell and shape timber before assembling clinker-built hulls with overlapping strakes. It is an unusually detailed image of organized eleventh-century labour, though not a step-by-step technical manual.

scenes.title: Ships Hauled to the Sea
scenes.latinInscription: hIC TRAhVNT NAVЄS AD MARЄ
scenes.englishTranslation: Here they haul ships to the sea.
scenes.summary: Teams drag completed hulls toward the water, turning construction into launch. Ropes, bodies and diagonal forms give the static embroidery a strong sense of exertion and forward motion.

annotations.title: Collective force
annotations.preview: The launch depends on coordinated human pulling rather than a named hero.
annotations.commentary: TRAHVNT supplies an active plural—'they haul'—while repeated bodies and lines of rope visualize the shared effort. The anonymous workforce is essential to the conquest's logistics.

annotations.title: Hull before rigging
annotations.preview: The craft are shown as beachable hulls that can be moved over land.
annotations.commentary: Their shallow, double-ended forms belong to a northern European shipbuilding tradition suited to landing on open shores. The embroidery simplifies scale and mechanics, so it should be read as informed representation rather than engineering specification.

scenes.title: Arms and Wine Are Loaded
scenes.latinInscription: ISTI PORTANT ARMAS AD NAVЄS ЄT hIC TRAhVNT CARRVM CVM VINO ET ARMIS
scenes.englishTranslation: These men carry arms to the ships, and here they haul a cart with wine and arms.
scenes.summary: Men carry armour and weapons toward the ships while others pull a cart laden with wine and military stores. The procession makes supply as visible as combat.

annotations.title: Armour carried, not worn
annotations.preview: Mail shirts, helmets and weapons travel separately to the ships.
annotations.commentary: The equipment is slung from poles or carried by hand. English Heritage notes the practical danger of wearing heavy armour aboard, while Owen-Crocker observes how this martial procession visually transforms Edward's earlier funeral procession.

annotations.title: Wine for an army
annotations.preview: The wheeled barrel makes provisioning part of the conquest story.
annotations.commentary: The titulus names wine twice as plainly as it names weapons: both are expedition necessities. Food, water, fodder and durable supplies are mostly implied, making the conspicuous barrel a memorable sign of organized transport.

scenes.title: William Crosses to Pevensey
scenes.latinInscription: † hIC VVILLELM DVX IN MAGNO NAVIGIO MARЄ TRANSIVIT ET VENIT AD PЄVЄNЄSÆ
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William crossed the sea in a great ship and came to Pevensey.
scenes.summary: William's fleet fills the main field and pushes into the borders as it crosses the Channel. The caption singles out the duke's 'great ship' and carries the action through to Pevensey in one continuous movement.

annotations.title: William's 'great ship'
annotations.preview: The caption distinguishes the commander's larger vessel from the fleet.
annotations.commentary: Later tradition calls William's flagship Mora, but that name is not embroidered here. It is safest to describe the richly marked vessel as the duke's great ship and treat the more specific identification as traditional rather than stated evidence.

annotations.title: A sea too large for the frame
annotations.preview: Masts and sails displace the usual upper-border ornament.
annotations.commentary: Owen-Crocker reads the fleet's incursion into the border as a way of enlarging both the sea and the invasion's significance. The third linen seam also falls between loading and embarkation, yet the makers disguise the structural join to preserve narrative flow.

scenes.title: Horses Disembark
scenes.latinInscription: hIC ЄXЄVNT CABALLI DE NAVIBVS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here horses come out of the ships.
scenes.summary: Horses leap or are led directly over the vessels' sides onto the Sussex shore. Their arrival converts a sea crossing into a mounted invasion.

annotations.title: Landing without a harbour
annotations.preview: The animals leave open boats directly onto the shore.
annotations.commentary: The shallow-draught ships could be beached, allowing horses to be unloaded without a built quay. The image conveys the difficulty and urgency of bringing cavalry across the Channel, although it compresses the actual procedure.

annotations.title: Travel tack
annotations.preview: The transported horses are controlled with simple halters rather than battle bridles.
annotations.commentary: Bouet notes that horses shown aboard the ships wear halters, a practical distinction from the fuller bridles and harness visible once mounted. Such details are valuable evidence, but the image remains selective and stylized.

scenes.title: Soldiers Ride to Seize Food
scenes.latinInscription: ЄT hIC MILITЄS FESTINAVERVNT hЄSTINGA VT CIBVM RAPERENTVR
scenes.englishTranslation: And here the soldiers hurried to Hastings so that food might be seized.
scenes.summary: Mounted soldiers race toward Hastings to requisition or plunder provisions. The caption openly connects military speed with the coercive supply needs of an invading army.

annotations.title: An embroidered gallop
annotations.preview: Outstretched legs and airborne bodies turn thread into speed.
annotations.commentary: Bouet identifies scene 40 as a clear example of the artists' convention for gallop: forelegs thrust forward, hind legs back and the body suspended. It is a graphic formula, but one grounded in close observation of equine movement.

annotations.title: Food taken by force
annotations.preview: RAPERENTVR means that food is to be seized or plundered.
annotations.commentary: This is not a neutral provisioning label: the verb makes coercion part of the official narrative. The following livestock, cooking and burning scenes show what invasion logistics cost the local population.

scenes.title: Wadard Oversees the Foraging
scenes.latinInscription: HIC EST VVADARD
scenes.englishTranslation: Here is Wadard.
scenes.summary: The mounted Wadard is singled out by name amid the collection and movement of supplies. Documents connect a Wadard with Bishop Odo, but the precise rank and narrative purpose of this embroidered figure remain debated.

annotations.title: Why name Wadard?
annotations.preview: A secondary knight receives the same naming privilege as major leaders.
annotations.commentary: Tsurushima examines Wadard with Turold and Vital, figures often linked to Odo and St Augustine's, Canterbury. The documentary associations are strong enough to matter, but they do not prove why this particular action was commemorated.

annotations.title: Livestock becomes supply
annotations.preview: Animals and burdens move leftward toward the army's kitchens.
annotations.commentary: Owen-Crocker connects this pillaged sheep and ox to an earlier procession in the embroidery, while Bouet draws attention to the smaller pack horse and its load. The sequence deliberately makes military appetite visible.

scenes.title: Meat Is Cooked and Served
scenes.latinInscription: hIC COQVITVR CARO ET hIC MINISTRAVЄRVNT MINISTRI
scenes.englishTranslation: Here meat is cooked, and here the servants have served.
scenes.summary: Cooks prepare meat while servants pass it onward toward the diners. The caption's repetition of the root ministr- tightly binds service as an action to the people performing it.

annotations.title: An army kitchen
annotations.preview: Fire, vessels and skewered meat turn plunder into a meal.
annotations.commentary: The embroidery gives unusually concrete attention to preparation rather than jumping from livestock to banquet. These everyday tools support the larger claim that the work preserves selective evidence for eleventh-century material practice.

annotations.title: MINISTRAVERVNT MINISTRI
annotations.preview: The servants 'served': a compact verbal echo in the Latin.
annotations.commentary: The cognate verb and noun make the line memorable while describing an orderly chain of labour. The official transcription preserves the material spelling and unusual E forms rather than normalizing them into classical Latin.

scenes.title: Odo Blesses the Feast
scenes.latinInscription: hIC FECЄRVNT PRANDIVM ET hIC EPISCOPVS  CIBVM ET POTVM BENEDICIT
scenes.englishTranslation: Here they made a meal, and here the bishop blesses the food and drink.
scenes.summary: The Norman leaders and soldiers gather to eat while Bishop Odo raises his hand in blessing over the food and drink. The scene joins sacred ritual to the practical consumption of captured provisions.

annotations.title: The bishop's blessing
annotations.preview: Odo makes the meal a formally sanctioned communal act.
annotations.commentary: The titulus identifies the officiant only by office—EPISCOPVS—but the surrounding narrative establishes Odo. His raised-hand pose has a close analogue in the Last Supper image of the St Augustine Gospels, a comparison central to arguments for Canterbury artistic connections.

annotations.title: Dining with distinction
annotations.preview: Vessels and seating help distinguish this Norman meal from the earlier Bosham feast.
annotations.commentary: De Vegvar shows that drinking vessels can operate as cultural markers within the embroidery's two major feasts. Their meaning is comparative and representational, not a complete inventory of what the army actually used.

scenes.title: Odo, William and Robert
scenes.latinInscription: ODO EPISCOPVS VVILLEM ROTBERT
scenes.englishTranslation: Bishop Odo, William, Robert.
scenes.summary: Three members of the ruling family sit in consultation: Bishop Odo, Duke William and Robert of Mortain. A sequence otherwise driven by verbs pauses to identify this elite council entirely by names.

annotations.title: A family council
annotations.preview: William is flanked by his maternal half-brothers Odo and Robert.
annotations.commentary: The trio concentrates military, ecclesiastical and comital authority in one image. Their explicit labels remove doubt about identity while still leaving the content of their discussion unstated.

annotations.title: Robert of Mortain
annotations.preview: ROT[B]ERT is usually identified as William's half-brother Robert, count of Mortain.
annotations.commentary: Spear's focused study places Robert within the embroidery's family politics and warns against treating apparently familiar identities as self-explanatory. The caption names Robert but does not supply his title.

scenes.title: The Fortification at Hastings
scenes.latinInscription:
ISTE IVSSIT VT FODERЄTVR CASTELLVM AD HESTENGA
CEASTRA
scenes.englishTranslation: This man ordered a fortification to be dug at Hastings. [Building label: “the camp”.]
scenes.summary: Men with digging tools raise an earthwork fortification at Hastings under orders from an unnamed 'this man.' The word CEASTRA is placed within the structure, turning the building itself into a label.

annotations.title: A castle is 'dug'
annotations.preview: FODERETVR emphasizes earthmoving rather than masonry.
annotations.commentary: The workers' tools and the verb point to an earth-and-timber campaign fortification, rendered through a compact visual convention. The image should not be read as a measured elevation of the actual Hastings castle.

annotations.title: CEASTRA inside the building
annotations.preview: An Old English-shaped word for a camp is stitched into the fortification.
annotations.commentary: CEASTRA is one of the inscription's conspicuously insular spellings and has been used in arguments for English production. Its uniquely cramped placement also records how the makers adapted text and image to limited space.

scenes.title: William Hears of Harold
scenes.latinInscription: HIC NVNTIATVM EST VVILLELM DE HAROLD
scenes.englishTranslation: Here it was reported to William concerning Harold.
scenes.summary: The caption says only that William received news about Harold; it does not specify the report.

annotations.title: Intelligence reaches the duke
annotations.preview: Gesture turns a silent encounter into reported speech.
annotations.commentary: NUNTIATVM EST is impersonal—'it was reported'—and the messenger remains unnamed. The British Museum's Stothard cast independently identifies this detail as William receiving a messenger.

annotations.title: Only 'about Harold'
annotations.preview: The caption names the topic, not the information conveyed.
annotations.commentary: DE HAROLD can cover news about Harold’s presence, army or movement. The stitched words do not supply a more exact message.

scenes.title: A House Is Burned
scenes.latinInscription: hIC DOMVS INCENDITVR
scenes.englishTranslation: Here a house is burned.
scenes.summary: Norman soldiers set fire to an occupied building while a woman and child flee. The compressed image gives civilian suffering an unusually direct place in the conquest narrative.

annotations.title: Ravaging made visible
annotations.preview: Flames turn the earlier search for food into unmistakable destruction.
annotations.commentary: The passive INCENDITVR does not name the burner in words, but the image embeds the event in William's advance through Sussex. Whether this records a specific house or stands for a broader campaign of ravaging is unknown.

annotations.title: A woman and child escape
annotations.preview: Two small figures make the cost of invasion personal.
annotations.commentary: Owen-Crocker links their escape compositionally to Conan's earlier flight from Dol, while stressing the border and main narrative's capacity for emotional counterpoint. Their names and individual circumstances are not recorded.

scenes.title: The Norman Army Rides to Battle
scenes.latinInscription: hIC MILITES EXIERVNT DE hESTENGA ET VENERVNT AD PRЄLIVM CONTRA hAROLDVM REGЄ
scenes.englishTranslation: Here the soldiers went out from Hastings and came to battle against King Harold.
scenes.summary: A dense body of mounted soldiers leaves Hastings and advances toward Harold's army. The long procession expands the story from local preparation into the decisive battle.

annotations.title: Eleven layers of cavalry
annotations.preview: Overlapping horses create the impression of disciplined depth.
annotations.commentary: Bouet analyzes scene 48 as an especially ambitious use of superimposition: partial heads and rumps imply ranks that the narrow strip cannot show literally. The result is ordered mass, not a count of the actual force.

annotations.title: Weapons point the way
annotations.preview: Inclined lances turn the cavalry column into directional force.
annotations.commentary: The riders' weapons project into the next action, one of the embroidery's recurring devices for pulling the eye forward. This compositional motion prepares the collision between mobile Norman forces and the English defensive line.

scenes.title: William Questions Vital
scenes.latinInscription: HIC VVILLELM DVX INTERROGAT VITAL SI VIDISSЄT EXERCITVM HAROLDI
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William asks Vital whether he had seen Harold's army.
scenes.summary: William pauses to question a named scout or knight, Vital, about the English army. The scene underscores reconnaissance immediately before contact.

annotations.title: Vital, named in the field
annotations.preview: The question names its informant but supplies no title for him.
annotations.commentary: Tsurushima treats Vital with Wadard and Turold, challenging easy assumptions that miles denotes one simple social class. A connection with Odo's circle is plausible, but the caption establishes only the name and the act of being questioned.

annotations.title: Reconnaissance before battle
annotations.preview: William asks whether Harold's army has been seen.
annotations.commentary: The indirect question SI VIDISSET makes uncertainty explicit at the narrative level. Both leaders are shown depending on riders and reports before the armies meet.

scenes.title: Harold Is Warned
scenes.latinInscription: ISTE NVNTIAT HAROLDVM RЄGEM DE EXERCITV VVILLILMI DVCIS
scenes.englishTranslation: This man reports to King Harold about the army of Duke William.
scenes.summary: An unnamed mounted messenger brings Harold news of William's approaching army. The matched intelligence scenes give both commanders knowledge just before battle.

annotations.title: 'This man' reports
annotations.preview: ISTE points to the messenger without preserving his name.
annotations.commentary: The demonstrative makes the image and caption work together: the viewer must look at the indicated rider. Unlike Vital in the previous scene, this intelligence-bearer is defined solely by his action.

annotations.title: Harold's ambling horse
annotations.preview: The unusual gait slows the visual tempo for the exchange of news.
annotations.commentary: Bouet identifies the mount in scene 50 as one of the embroidery's rare depictions of an amble. The controlled gait contrasts with the galloping advance and helps isolate a moment of communication.

scenes.title: William Addresses His Army
scenes.latinInscription: HIC VVILLELM DVX ALLOQVITVR SVIS MILITIBVS VT PREPARARENT SE VIRILITER ET SAPIENTER AD PRELIVM CONTRA ANGLORVM EXERCITVM
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Duke William addresses his soldiers so that they might prepare themselves manfully and wisely for battle against the army of the English.
scenes.summary: William exhorts his troops to prepare courageously and prudently before the battle begins. The unusually long caption slows the advance long enough to frame the combat as ordered and purposeful.

annotations.title: A speech stitched in indirect form
annotations.preview: The caption reports William's purpose rather than quoting his words.
annotations.commentary: ALLOQVITVR introduces the address, followed by a purpose clause. VIRILITER ET SAPIENTER balances courage with judgment, constructing an ideal of disciplined command before violence erupts.

annotations.title: The army arranged for attack
annotations.preview: Archers, infantry and mounted knights belong to different phases of the Norman assault.
annotations.commentary: English Heritage reconstructs William's normal order as archers forward, infantry next and cavalry behind. The embroidery is a narrative image rather than a tactical plan, but its contrasts of troop type and movement are central to the battle's visual logic.

scenes.title: Leofwine and Gyrth Fall
scenes.latinInscription: hIC CЄCIDЄRVNT LEVVINE ЄT GYRÐ FRATRES hAROLDI REGIS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here fell Leofwine and Gyrth, brothers of King Harold.
scenes.summary: The battle claims Harold's brothers Leofwine and Gyrth, whose deaths the caption singles out by name and kinship. Individual identification within the compressed melee is less secure than the verbal statement.

annotations.title: Leofwine's possible last stand
annotations.preview: A mailed axeman struck from behind is commonly associated with Leofwine.
annotations.commentary: Davis notes that repeating a figure can represent successive action, so the falling warrior nearby may show the same man twice. The caption guarantees Leofwine's death in the scene, but not a perfectly unambiguous one-to-one label over every body.

annotations.title: Which figure is Gyrth?
annotations.preview: The name sits over combatants whose individual identities are debated.
annotations.commentary: Davis finds it unclear whether Gyrth is the swordsman or spearman beneath the inscription. The caption establishes his death in this scene, but the mapping between name and individual figure remains uncertain.

scenes.title: English and French Fall Together
scenes.latinInscription: hIC CЄCIDERVNT SIMVL ANGLI ЄT FRANCI IN PRELIO
scenes.englishTranslation: Here English and French fell together in battle.
scenes.summary: The embroidery widens the slaughter across the central field and lower border as men and horses fall on both sides. The caption's SIMVL insists on simultaneous losses rather than a simple one-sided triumph.

annotations.title: Horses in catastrophic motion
annotations.preview: Rearing and overturning mounts make the instability of battle visible.
annotations.commentary: Bouet analyzes the beige and blue-black horses in this scene as carefully chosen moments of imbalance and collapse. Their bodies register violence that affects animals as well as human combatants.

annotations.title: The border becomes battlefield
annotations.preview: Dismembered bodies replace ornament below the main action.
annotations.commentary: Owen-Crocker argues that corpses invading the lower border amplify the conflict from heroic encounter into shared pain and chaos. The formal frame can no longer contain the violence.

scenes.title: Odo Rallies the Troops
scenes.latinInscription: HIC ODO EPISCOPVS BACVLVM TЄNЄNS CONFORTAT PVEROS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here Bishop Odo, holding a staff, encourages the young men.
scenes.summary: Bishop Odo rides into the crisis holding a staff and rallying the Norman fighters. The caption makes a churchman, rather than William, the agent who restores courage at this moment.

annotations.title: A bishop's staff
annotations.preview: The caption calls Odo's object a BACVLVM, a staff or club.
annotations.commentary: Its wording distinguishes the object from a sword or lance while still placing Odo physically inside battle. Explanations that the club neatly avoids clerical bloodshed are traditional but should not be presented as proven motive.

annotations.title: Who are the PVEROS?
annotations.preview: The Latin literally says 'boys' or 'young men,' not children in the modern sense.
annotations.commentary: In context the word refers to the fighting followers Odo encourages. Translating it as 'troops' captures function, while 'young men' stays closer to the stitched vocabulary; either choice should be explained.

scenes.title: William Reveals His Face
scenes.latinInscription:
hIC EST DVX VVILLELM
E[...]TIVS
scenes.englishTranslation: Here is Duke William. E[…]tius [name incomplete].
scenes.summary: William lifts his helmet to reveal his face. This is commonly connected with accounts of a rumour that he had been killed. A second, damaged name is often reconstructed as Eustace, but both that reading and the adjacent figure’s identity remain uncertain.

annotations.title: 'Here is Duke William'
annotations.preview: William exposes his face so the troops can recognize that he lives.
annotations.commentary: English Heritage relates the scene to a battlefield panic caused by a rumour of William's death. The embroidery turns recognition into a decisive act of command: identity itself becomes a rallying signal.

annotations.title: E[…]TIVS: Eustace?
annotations.preview: A fragmentary name has encouraged a famous but uncertain identification.
annotations.commentary: The pointing standard-bearer is often called Eustace of Boulogne, yet Spear stresses that the reconstruction is tentative and that the area has a complicated restoration history. Both the name’s restoration and the figure’s identification remain uncertain.

scenes.title: The French Fight On
scenes.latinInscription: hIC FRANCI PVGNANT ET CЄCIDЄRVNT QVI ЄRANT CVM hAROLDO
scenes.englishTranslation: Here the French fight, and those who were with Harold fell.
scenes.summary: Mounted attackers renew their assault and Harold's companions fall around the English position. The caption calls the continental fighters FRANCI, a broader label than 'Normans.'

annotations.title: Why 'the French'?
annotations.preview: FRANCI names the attackers collectively rather than restricting them to Normans.
annotations.commentary: William's host included contingents from beyond Normandy, and the final captions contrast ANGLI with FRANCI. The word's exact social and political range is contextual; translating it simply as 'Normans' would erase the stitched wording.

annotations.title: Cavalry against a standing line
annotations.preview: Mounted mobility presses against English fighters who defend on foot.
annotations.commentary: The embroidery makes cavalry and infantry visually distinct, while English Heritage cautions that the battle involved repeated assaults and reversals rather than one clean charge. The depiction is narratively forceful but selective.

scenes.title: King Harold Is Killed
scenes.latinInscription: hIC Harold REX INTERFЄCTVS EST
scenes.englishTranslation: Here King Harold was killed.
scenes.summary: The caption announces Harold's death across two adjacent violent figures: one grasps at a shaft near his face, while another is cut down by a mounted swordsman. Which figure represents Harold—and whether the two show successive moments of one death—remains one of the tapestry's central disputes.

annotations.title: The arrow-in-the-eye figure
annotations.preview: The most famous identification is not secure.
annotations.commentary: The standing figure beneath HAROLD appears to handle a shaft at the face, supporting the familiar arrow story. Foys argues from early reproductions, restoration and caption placement that this figure was not originally Harold receiving an eye-shot; other accounts remain possible.

annotations.title: The falling figure
annotations.preview: INTERFЄCTVS EST lies over a warrior struck down by a mounted attacker.
annotations.commentary: Foys identifies this sword-struck figure as the stronger candidate for Harold, while another reading treats both figures as successive images of the king’s death. The surviving image does not collapse these alternatives into a single certainty.

scenes.title: The English Flee
scenes.latinInscription: ET FVGA VERTERVNT ANGLI
scenes.englishTranslation: And the English turned in flight.
scenes.summary: The defeated English break away under pursuit, and the surviving embroidery ends in flight rather than William's coronation. Both the damaged physical ending and the restoration history of its final caption make this apparent conclusion provisional.

annotations.title: A leaderless retreat
annotations.preview: English fighters turn away as Norman riders pursue.
annotations.commentary: English Heritage describes Harold's death as the decisive loss after which the English line gave way. The embroidery ends the extant action with bodies moving off to the right, maintaining momentum beyond the surviving cloth.

annotations.title: This was probably not the ending
annotations.preview: The embroidery's physical termination is lost, and the final titulus is heavily restored.
annotations.commentary: Owen-Crocker notes that the missing conclusion is often imagined as William’s accession, which would answer the enthroned king at the opening, but that reconstruction remains hypothetical. Musset judges ET FVGA VERTERVNT ANGLI a later restoration, so the surviving appearance cannot establish eleventh-century certainty.
